inline.s: (Original title: Layman Jin Yixiang Sees Amitabha and Passes Away Peacefully)
Layman Jin Yixiang lived on Chongqing South Road in Shanghai. He was a doctor and worked in a hospital for close on twenty years, and retired in
. In
, in the
seventh
month, on the
26th day,
at six in the afternoon he passed away, aged seventy-six.

Early in life the layman took up the Buddhist faith. He lost his wife in middle age, and after retirement he kept a lifelong vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha's name. He often held seven-day Buddha-recitation retreats at home by himself, rising at half past three every morning to bow to the Buddha and recite his name, and resting only at eight or nine in the evening. At night he sat in meditation and often slept in his clothes. Even in illness he insisted on bowing to the Buddha, and stopped only when his sickness grew severe and he truly could not move. He constantly read and recited the great vehicle sutras, such as the Lotus Sutra, the Śūraṅgama Sutra, and the Diamond Sutra, and took the Amitabha Sutra, the Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra, the Chapter on Pure Conduct, and the Heart of the Śūraṅgama Mantra as his regular daily practice. He lived frugally, and all his spare money went to printing and giving away sutras, buying living creatures for release, and making offerings to the Three Jewels. At the end of his life he still had over eight hundred yuan left, and he used it all for life release.

The layman never read novels, never went to the theatre, and never watched television. He said: “Our time is short, and there is not even enough of it for our practice — how could we have time to look at such things?”

When the layman's illness became critical he went to the hospital for examination: blood tests, urine and stool tests, blood pressure, ultrasound, electrocardiogram — all were normal, showing that his body was free of the suffering of illness.

Five days before his death, Layman Yan Hongxing came to visit him and said, “Your illness will get better.” The layman replied, “I have already seen Amitabha Buddha; I am going to be reborn in the West.” Two days before his death he said to his son, “Today and tomorrow you will attend to me; the day after tomorrow you will not need to.” And indeed at six in the afternoon of the third day he passed away. As he was dying his son urged him to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. He said, “That you wish me to recover is your filial love, but I shall single-mindedly recite Amitabha Buddha and seek the Western Land.” Then, amid the sound of Buddha-recitation, he cried aloud once, “Amitabha Buddha,” and passed away peacefully. Twenty-six hours after his passing his whole body had grown cold, yet the crown of his head was still warm. After thirty-four hours his four limbs were supple, bending and stretching freely, just as in life. From these auspicious signs — his foreknowledge of the time and the rest — it is plain that his rebirth in the West was no empty thing.
Recorded by his sons Zhiguang and Zhijiong
(Original title: Layman Deng Zhenshan's Diligent Practice Draws Heavenly Music to Welcome Him)

The Pure Land Dharma gate covers all three capacities. Even a humble townsman who knows few characters and does not understand profound Buddhist principle, if he can deeply believe in the Western Land, recite the Buddha's name in earnest, and do whatever good deeds lie within his power whenever and wherever he can, will certainly be received by the Buddha at the end of his life and be reborn in the West. The story of the passing of the aged layman Deng Zhenshan is proof of this.

Master Xinguang of the Kaifeng Buddhist Association brought back from Zhengzhou a piece of thrilling good news: the story of how the aged layman Deng Zhenshan foreknew the time of his death and how heavenly music resounded in the sky as he passed away.
Layman Deng Zhenshan was born in

, on the first day of the second month, into a peasant family. His ancestral home was at Caomenguan in Kaifeng, Henan. He lost his father at the age of nine, was raised by his mother, and later moved to Zhengzhou. As a grown man he did odd jobs and made his living from cosmetics and general merchandise.
he took up formal employment as a worker at the Zhengzhou Paint Factory.

As a child living in Kaifeng he often went to the Three-Corner Shrine of the Shifang Cloister to hear the Dharma masters expound the sutras and to watch the masters chant, circumambulate the Buddha, and perform Buddhist rites; from early boyhood he felt a fondness for Buddhism.

he received the Three Refuges at the Henan Buddhist Study Society in Kaifeng and brought home many bronze images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to venerate. Every day he bowed and recited his devotions without a single break, becoming a devout Buddhist.

The layman came from hard circumstances and had a deep understanding of poverty and illness, so he constantly gave according to his means and his strength — for instance, giving away plasters, eye medicines, and other remedies to relieve the sick of their pain. In winter he gave away cotton garments to keep others warm; in summer he set out tea by the roadside in front of his own gate to slake the thirst of passers-by. His spirit of delighting in goodness and generosity won the praise of the local people.

he retired on account of illness and went to live within the compound of the Zhengzhou Buddhist Study Society, where he strove diligently, bowing to the Buddha and chanting sutras. He did not rest until two in the morning, and to the very moment of his death he was still fingering his recitation beads.
It was in
, in the
eighth
month, on the
17th,

at seven in the morning that he passed away. The day before, he instructed his family, saying: “I have nearly finished reciting the Buddha's name and shall soon be going. You must keep the Buddha's rules and precepts well, protect the true Dharma, and be true Buddhists. From today, recite the Buddha's name for me day and night without stopping.” His sons and daughters did as he asked and sat around his bed reciting for him. Strangely, the Zhengzhou Buddhist Study Society had for many years housed no monks, yet nine monks suddenly appeared: Masters Zhenkuo, Nengxian, Zhengru, Yanwei, Renwu, Hongchang, Renqun, and others. These masters did not stop to rest but at once joined the local lay Buddhists in the recitation. By seven o'clock the next morning, Layman Deng, amid the sound of the assembly reciting the Buddha's name, departed for the West.

At that time, in the sky above the Zhengzhou Buddhist Study Society, there suddenly came the sounds of drums and music, of Sanskrit chanting, and of Buddha-recitation. The sound was melodious and clear, sweet and pleasing to the ear, truly ringing through the clear sky. The masters and lay Buddhists taking part in the recitation all heard it. At first they thought someone was playing a tape; later they sensed that the sound came from the sky. Everyone was moved and full of praise — it was rare beyond words — and each recited the Buddha's name with even greater single-minded earnestness. This wondrous heavenly music lasted until half past ten before it stopped. Afterwards everyone regretted that they had been so intent on reciting that they had not recorded it on tape in time.

The aged layman Deng Zhenshan was only an ordinary Buddhist, yet at his death he could show such auspicious signs. This proves that the Buddha's vows are not empty: so long as we ordinarily possess faith and vows and recite the Buddha's name and do good with utmost sincerity, we will certainly attain rebirth in the West. Layman Deng is truly a fine example for us to learn from. Those who walk the Pure Land path may grasp the meaning in their hearts.
Recorded by Shi Xinguang and Jiang Foqing,
, in the
third
month
(Original title: Layman Zhao Chengzhang Reaches the Other Shore Through a Single Sincere Thought)
One day in the
year 1987
, in the
third

month, I went to Zhejiang No. 1 Hospital to be treated for a cold. While I sat on a bench waiting for the nurse to call my number, reading the Buddhist book Master Yinguang's Dharma Words, a man of about
sixty

years of age suddenly came over, pointed at me, and said: “You look like a hopeless case of superstition — coming to a hospital and still reading that kind of book!” I answered him, “This is not superstition; it is right faith, it is wise faith.” He asked, “Then what good does believing in the Buddha do you?” I told him briefly, “One who truly believes in the Buddha and recites his name enjoys peace and good fortune in life, and at death is received by the Buddha and reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.” He retorted, “What real example can you give to prove that one who believes in the Buddha and recites his name can be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss?”

So I briefly told him how my mother-in-law had foreknown that she would pass away on the eighth day of the fourth month, and how when the day came she indeed passed away, free of illness and suffering, sitting in a wicker chair reciting the Buddha's name. When he heard this he said, half believing and half doubting, “All right — where do you live? I will go and investigate.”

A few days later, as fate would have it, I ran into him again at Zhejiang No. 1 Hospital. The moment he saw me he came over and sat down beside me, saying, “What you told me last time was indeed true. A few hours before your mother-in-law passed away she was still holding my little aunt's child for her.” As we talked I learned that he was in fact the husband of my factory colleague Sister Qiaoyun, that his name was Zhao Chengzhang, and that after their marriage they lived on Changqing Street. Sister Qiaoyun believed in Buddhism and kept images of the Three Sages at home, bowing and reciting the Buddha's name morning and evening, while her husband Zhao Chengzhang leaned toward Christianity and did not believe in Buddhism.

Later I learned that Zhao Chengzhang's illness was incurable, and that after a stay in hospital he had gone home to convalesce. So I went to his house to visit him, but his wife Sister Qiaoyun stopped me and asked me not to go into his bedroom to see him. Her reason was that after Zhao Chengzhang came home, under the so-called persuasion of several of his friends, he had formally joined the “Jesus” faith, saying that after death he would go to heaven, and that he now even wore a small iron cross on his chest. We were sorry to hear that he had taken a wrong step. But since we had come, we took a look from his doorway.

A few days later I met Sister Qiaoyun, who said to me happily, “What a strange thing! Just before the end, my Chengzhang suddenly asked me for the holy image of ‘Amitabha Buddha’ that I recite before. I said to him, You belong to Jesus and will go to heaven after death — what do you want with an Amitabha Buddha image? Reciting the Buddha's name is for rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; they are two utterly different roads. When he heard this he pleaded earnestly, ‘I do not want to go to the kingdom of heaven. I want to go to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.’ So I told him, ‘If that is what you want, then hurry and single-mindedly recite Amitabha Buddha — there is still time.’ He was delighted to hear it, and without the least hesitation joined his palms at once and began to recite the holy name of Amitabha Buddha. I recited along with him to assist, and after about ten minutes Chengzhang slowly lowered his hands, and with a smile on his face passed away peacefully.”

Sister Qiaoyun is a devout disciple who has taken refuge; she keeps holy images at home and bows and recites the Buddha's name morning and evening. Though her husband Chengzhang believed in “Jesus,” he had long been steeped in the influence of his wife's Buddha-recitation, and the seeds of the Land of Nurturing had quietly been sown in the field of his eighth consciousness. It was also owing to his deep good roots and karmic conditions that he repeatedly met the good teacher Meng Zongzhen in the hospital, whose propagation of the Dharma and guidance nourished him; and so at the end of his life his good roots came forth, he resolutely abandoned his former faith, joined his palms, recited the Buddha's name, and sought rebirth in the Pure Land. In the Chapter on Perfect Penetration through Buddha-Recitation of Great Strength Bodhisattva it is taught: “The Tathāgatas of the ten directions pity and remember living beings as a mother remembers her child. If the child runs away, what use is the mother's remembering? But if the child remembers the mother as the mother remembers the child, then mother and child will not be far apart through life after life. If the minds of living beings remember the Buddha and recite the Buddha's name, they will certainly see the Buddha now or hereafter….” We afflicted living beings have only to remember the Buddha and recite his name; no matter what our past has been, we can, like Zhao Chengzhang, through a single sincere thought at the moment of death, receive the Buddha's compassionate regard and give up this life with a smile. Therefore I respectfully counsel my fellow practitioners of Buddha-recitation: recite the great name diligently and seek birth in the Land of Nurturing!
Spoken by Meng Shouzhen of Hangzhou,
, in the
first
month, respectfully noted by Miaoyuan
(Original title: Deaf Peng Recites the Buddha's Name Sincerely, Takes Leave of the Assembly, and Is Born in the West Sitting Upright)

When I was working at a large cotton cloth shop in Hangzhou there was a handyman there of over fifty, ugly of face, with slightly drooping eyes, a twisted mouth that drooled, unclear speech, and hard of hearing — a man whose looks invited dislike. He emptied the spittoons, swept the floor, and did the cleaning and other odd jobs in the shop. No one paid him much attention, and no one even knew his name; everyone called him “Deaf Peng.” His old wife also washed and mended clothes for the shop's unmarried staff, and on that they barely got by. Strangely enough, though this “Deaf Peng” could not read and spoke indistinctly, when he chanted the Heart Sutra and the holy name of “Amitabha Buddha” on the fourth floor of the shop in the morning, I could hear him very clearly from below, every sound resounding, every phrase full of power. That a man who could not read should be able to recite the Heart Sutra from memory, and that his Buddha-recitation should be so clear and rhythmic, struck me at the time as merely curious.
In

1948, in the spring, one day the boss happened to come up to the woollen goods department of the shop for a short rest. Somehow “Deaf Peng” got wind of it and came right after him. Seeing the boss, he at once knelt on the ground and bowed respectfully, murmuring, “Thank you, boss, for taking me in.” The next morning and noon there was no sign of “Deaf Peng”; only in the afternoon did his old wife come to the shop and tell us: “After Deaf Peng went home yesterday, this man who was always dirty and never cared about cleanliness wanted to go to the Weiquan Pool bathhouse at Baoyoufang to bathe, and he even changed into a new set of longtou cloth underclothes. Before going to sleep he told me to sleep in the outer room tonight, and before the meal I heard him reciting the Buddha's name. At daybreak I pushed the door open and saw that Deaf Peng had already died sitting upright, a kind and gentle smile on his face, the cotton quilt drawn up neatly over him….” When we heard this, we recalled how the day before he had suddenly bowed to the boss in thanks, gone to the bathhouse, told his wife to sleep in the outer room, and then died peacefully without illness — it seemed there had been some forewarning. Some said, “This is the benefit of reciting the Buddha's name.” Others said, “It was probably a heart attack.” I thought: if he had died of a sudden illness, why was there a smile on his face and no sign of suffering? So my mind remained in doubt, until later I read such books as Returning from the Forked Road and What Must Be Known at the Time of Death, and realized that this is the mark of one who recites the Buddha's name being reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. I have written this down especially.
Miaofa of Hangzhou,
, in the
third
month
(Original title: At the Point of Death Layman Wang Atang Gives Off Fragrance and a Lotus Appears in the Cremation)

Layman Wang Atang of Tianhu Village, Luotuo Town, Zhenhai District, Ningbo, was a tailor by trade, nicknamed “Swift Tailor.” He had two sons and two daughters. From childhood he was diligent and thrifty; because his children did not turn out as he wished, he felt that life is full of suffering and began to believe in Buddhism. After his children married and set up households, all his earnings went into making Buddha and Bodhisattva images in nunneries as meritorious deeds. Though he had eaten vegetarian for sixty years, he had never known to recite the Buddha's name and seek the Western Land. From the age of seventy-two he made a vow to keep up morning and evening devotions and to recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, seeking to leave the Sahā world and be reborn in the Western Pure Land as soon as possible. He lived simply and plainly, caring nothing for fine clothes, food, housing, or travel, and after his devotions he went back to his tailoring. At first he bowed to the Buddha an hour in the morning and an hour in the evening; gradually he increased it to eight hours in all. His Buddha hall was the upper floor of a dilapidated plank house facing west, colder than elsewhere in winter and hotter than elsewhere in summer. Yet he rose at three every morning to bow to the Buddha and began his evening devotions at four in the afternoon, eight years without a single day's break, through bitter winter and scorching summer. Although he had labour insurance enough to live on, he still sewed clothes for others during the day, and gave all his earnings to the support of Buddhist temples and to charity. Because his eyesight had not failed and he needed no glasses, and because his body suffered no illness, he worked right up to the end of his life at eighty, never resting a single day.

In the ninth month of the lunar calendar last year he came to the various lotus friends in Luotuo Town and said, “I am afraid I shall pass away this year. Please, all of you lotus friends, recite the Buddha's name for me when the time comes!” On the twelfth day of the twelfth month his son-in-law came to my house and said, “My father-in-law is unwell.” The next day I went to Tianhu Village, five li away, to visit him. At the time he said, “I am not going yet; when I go I will send word to you.” Because I was uneasy, I went to see him again on the fifteenth without waiting for his notice. I found him lying in bed with his palms joined, reciting the Buddha's name aloud with all his might, his countenance as usual and no sign of illness to be seen. I asked whether he was in pain. He said, “I am not ill.” But his old wife said he had not eaten for three days. I had brought a tape recording, but he said there was no need to play it just then. Seeing that his mind was clear, I thought he would not be going for the time being, and so took my leave. But as I was leaving I instructed his daughter: if there should be any change, the recording must be played to assist the recitation, and I and our fellow practitioners must be sent for at once. Not long after I got home, at half past four in the afternoon of the sixteenth, his son-in-law came and said to me, “My father-in-law is about to pass away; please come quickly.” So I took my clothes and set out with him. Because he had notified the other lotus friends first and came to me last, I rode on the back of his bicycle to his father-in-law's house. To my surprise the aged layman had already passed away; I saw only a house full of family members holding incense and kneeling in recitation to see him off. I joined them and the tape recorder in the recitation. Although Layman Wang had already stopped breathing, his face was as it had been in life. According to his daughter: “From the time my father took to his bed, except when sleeping, he recited the Buddha's name aloud the whole time, right up to four o'clock this afternoon, never once crying out in pain, until he stopped breathing at a quarter past four.

That night I and two other lay Buddhists, together with his children, recited the Buddha's name until after two in the morning, when the layman's son and son-in-law washed and changed him. When the covering quilt was lifted, everyone smelled a pure fragrance. The layman's whole body was still soft and slightly warm, not in the least like that of a man ten hours dead; all who had come to assist in the recitation marvelled that they had never seen the like. Then we recited the Buddha's name aloud until the clothes had been changed, after which we took turns assisting the recitation until the next morning, when the body was taken for cremation. During the cremation, one of the women assisting saw a white lotus flower emerge from the cremation chamber. From the case of Layman Wang we may know that if only we deeply believe the Buddha's words, vow earnestly to be reborn, recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, and strive without slackening, then at the end of life we will surely foreknow the time, be free of the suffering of illness, and be reborn in Amitabha's Pure Land.
Su Keming of Luotuo Town, Zhenhai,
, in the
sixth
month, on the
8th
day

blocks.text: 56. Passing to the West with a Smile

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Yan Zihui Recites the Buddha's Name Earnestly, Smiles, and Keeps a Warm Crown)

My late father, whose taboo name was Zihui, was by constitution healthy, fond of work, and seldom ill. Apart from drinking wine, he was frugal in clothes and food and had no other habits. This summer was strangely hot, the damp heat oppressive. My father first developed a heat boil on his cheek, and later a slight one appeared on his back as well. Everyone supposed it was the heat boils spreading, never suspecting that the poison had its root there. My father was by nature quiet and well disciplined; whatever the matter or the ailment, he would never speak of it to others, and so several days were lost, until at the autumn festival the affected place gradually swelled. Physicians of both internal and external medicine were called and treated him one after another, and he suffered greatly. We unfilial ones, seeing this, grieved beyond measure, wishing to take his place and unable to. So we devoutly besought our Buddha to grant him early recovery.

By the twenty-eighth day of the sixth month the external symptoms seemed to have healed, but after all, his years were advanced and his strength failed him. At noon on the twenty-ninth his breathing became laboured, yet his mind was very clear and his speech as usual. Around five in the afternoon we saw that my father had the intention of departing. I at once sounded the bell and recited aloud the six-character great name, and with our family recited in unison to assist. I asked at my father's ear whether he heard the Buddha's name. He said he heard it very distinctly, and comforted me, saying that he had put everything down and was reciting the Buddha's name in peace. At six fifty he passed away to the West with a smile on his face, leaving us unfilial ones behind. After I had knelt reciting the Buddha's name, I felt him: his hands and feet were cold, but the crown of his head was very warm. My father recited the Buddha's name earnestly in ordinary life, and now at death the auspicious signs were thus; surely by the Buddha's compassion his spirit has returned to the Pure Realm. I have set down the facts as they are for all my fellow practitioners of the Pure Land.
Dai Dichen

blocks.text: 57. Passing to the West with a Laugh

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Huang Nianzu Expounds the Dharma of the Six Sutras and Passes to the West with a Laugh)
The aged layman Huang Nianzu was born in

, on the sixth day of the third month of the guichou year. He lost his father early, and as a boy often accompanied his mother, the Lady Mei, to hear sutras and the Dharma, and received the nurture of his uncle, the senior Buddhist scholar Layman Mei Guangxi, so that his aspirations stood above the common. He took refuge with the great Chan master Xuyun, and studied esoteric methods under the great Red School master Wang Lianhua Zhengjue and the great White School master Guru Gongga. After the victory of the War of Resistance he paid his respects to the great Pure Land master Layman Xia Lianju and became his personal disciple. He delved into the teachings and strove diligently in practice, attaining great and profound accomplishment in the exoteric, the esoteric, Chan, and Pure Land. To repay the Buddha's grace and his teachers' grace,
from 1979

the layman read through the whole range of literature, pondering it with painstaking care, and over six years wrote the Explanation of the Mahāyāna Sutra of Immeasurable Life (abbreviated as the Explanation of the Great Sutra), which circulated at home and abroad. While writing, the old man several times lectured and spread the Dharma at the Chinese Buddhist Academy, the Lay Buddhists' Forest, and Guanghua Temple. Besides the Explanation of the Great Sutra he also wrote Provisions for the Pure Land, Collected Echoes of the Valley, Lectures on the Huayan Treatise on Buddha-Recitation Samādhi, and A Record of the Heart's Voice.

The old man's main task this year was to complete the Vernacular Explanation of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life. He said: “The Explanation of the Great Sutra that I wrote before was aimed at the level of those who expound the Dharma; people of ordinary level and ordinary capacity cannot read it. Once the Vernacular Explanation comes out, a great many living beings will benefit from it!” Therefore, heedless of his eighty years and his frail, ailing body, he threw himself into writing. This Vernacular Explanation is by no means merely the Explanation of the Great Sutra rendered into plain speech; on the basis of the Explanation of the Great Sutra it uses a vernacular form, cutting the cumbersome and keeping the simple, highlighting the essential points, not only preserving the original depth but making great breakthroughs as well. Many passages of surpassing brilliance are not to be found in the Explanation of the Great Sutra; in concise and popular language it enables people to believe and accept Amitabha's inconceivable one-vehicle ocean of vows, which transcends feeling and views, and the six-character great name, and so gain true benefit. Sadly, the book was written only up to the beginning of the chapter on rebirth in the three grades when the old man passed away. Yet everywhere in the book the Huayan realm of non-obstruction among phenomena and non-obstruction between principle and phenomena is made manifest; though the chapters are incomplete, the meaning is perfectly round. Now his personal disciples, to fulfil the old man's vow to save living beings, are hurrying to put the manuscript in order.

Every day, besides rushing to write the great sutra, the old man had also to complete his own fixed daily practice (reciting forty to fifty thousand Buddha-mantras a day, and performing at least one great ritual). Besides counting these, he recited at loose moments as well. So he could not go to sleep until after one in the morning every day. The old man often said: “Nothing whatever may crowd out Buddha-recitation!” He had been vegetarian for many years and gave no thought to caring for his body, so his food was always poor; at lunch especially, when the family were out at day work, he would himself throw the leftovers from the night before into one pot and eat a bowl of thin vegetable rice gruel — and even this gruel was often burnt, for he was single-minded in writing and constantly forgot what was on the fire. Once his grandson Bai Zhen smelled burnt rice in the courtyard and wondered whose rice had burnt; sniffing more carefully, he traced it to his grandfather's room. He pushed the door open at once: the room was full of smoke. The boy's heart clenched, for he knew his grandfather never left the room and had heart disease; such thick smoke and he had not noticed it — it must be that his heart trouble had flared up. When the frightened boy turned his head to look at the desk, his eyes suddenly filled with tears. To repay the Buddha's great grace, to spread the Dharma, to save living beings, the old man was utterly self-forgetful as he wrote, not in the least aware of the pungent smoke. The grandson said through his tears, “This gruel can't be eaten.” But he laughed and said, “This food is quite good; don't spend energy and time on what you eat.” Then he filled a bowl with the blackish vegetable gruel and ate it with relish, laughing as he said, “I am living the life of an immortal now; I would not trade lives with anyone. What is the joy of human life? It is the joy of the Dharma!” To write the vernacular explanation of the great sutra, the old man truly reached the point of forgetting food and sleep.
In the
third
month, from the
16th
through the
18th

day, the old man lectured one person on the Dharma for three days running, speaking late each day. This crowded out much of the time he had meant for Buddha-recitation, so at night he had to work overtime to finish his fixed practice, and these few days he slept even later. He suddenly felt a discomfort in his throat. Sitting on the edge of the bed to take medicine, he picked up the medicine in his hand and was already dozing; a nod of sleep came over him and he fell from the bedside, striking the edge of a chair. Yet the old man did not make a sound; he endured the severe pain and, with a fortitude beyond imagining, felt his way in the dark back onto the bed. The next morning he told his family with a laugh, “I fell last night.” None of them believed it; they thought he was joking. Only when he was examined later did they learn that his thigh bone was comminuted and fractured, and that a large dark purple bruise had appeared on the injured thigh. Even so, the old man said, “At my age, whether the leg heals or not does not matter; fortunately my mind still works and my hands can move. Even if I am paralysed in bed, I will finish the Vernacular Explanation.” This fall brought on the recurrence of many of his old illnesses; heart, lungs, and kidneys all deteriorated. All his life the old man had never had time to go to hospital for treatment, let alone be hospitalized. It was only for the sake of finishing the Vernacular Explanation that he made an exception and agreed to be taken to hospital, to make one last effort.

When his disciples at home and abroad heard of it and wanted to come and attend on him, the old man wired back: “No one is permitted to come. All of you recite the Buddha's name where you are, and simply pray that I may finish the Vernacular Explanation.”
In the
third
month, on the

26th, at noon, the old man's condition worsened. He opened his mouth a few times but could no longer speak. Then, utterly detached and at ease, he smiled, so that everyone felt: “There is nothing left in his heart at all; he is perfectly light and free.” After that he gave no further sign until
the third
month, on the
27th
, before dawn, at
he passed away.

Late that night the body was carried to his home. His family and his disciples from home and abroad recited the Buddha's name day and night for seven days. The weather was hot and no preservative measures whatever were taken, yet the remains not only gave off no unpleasant odour — many people smelled a rare fragrance.
On the
fourth
month, the

7th, the body was cremated. It was by then the twelfth day since his death. When the body was lifted it felt soft, the fingers could still be moved, and it seemed clearly lighter, giving off a rare fragrance from time to time.

After the cremation, the recitation beads the old man had carried with him passed through the great fire unspoiled, and his relics were white as jade. From the ashes were gathered, one after another, more than three hundred śarīra relics in five colours (red, yellow, white, green, and black) — in fact the total exceeded three hundred.
(Note: The contents of this article have been written concisely and factually on the basis of the letter and materials sent to me by Layman Bai Zhen.)
Respectfully recorded by Miaoxiang,
, in the
fourth
month, on the
26th
day

blocks.text: 58. Passing to the West in Peace

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Gu Yanyou's Whole Family Believes in the Buddha and Will Meet in the Land of Ultimate Bliss)
Layman Gu Tingyou,

on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, took refuge with the aged Dharma Master Anxi of Jile Temple in Harbin and was given the Dharma name Guoxing. All his life the layman delighted in goodness and generosity, never counting personal gain or loss. When others were in difficulty he always helped with all his strength. Whenever there were good works — building temples, giving charity, offering vegetarian feasts to the Sangha, Dharma assemblies, making Buddha images, printing sutras, his daughter's pilgrimage to the mountains — he always contributed generously. Yet his own life was always frugal: plain cloth and vegetarian food, coarse tea and simple meals. After retirement he did voluntary work for the Buddhist Association and the temples, delivering rice, flour, and clothing. To everyone he met he spoke of the blessedness and adornment of the Land of Ultimate Bliss and of the real benefits of Buddha-recitation and rebirth there, practising the gift of Dharma and converting living beings. In his later years the layman devoted himself exclusively to the Pure Land; in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down he recited the Buddha's name without interruption. If there was fine food, to offer it first to the Buddha and the Sangha was what he most loved and most delighted in.

In the years before my father took refuge in the Buddhist gate his health was poor; he suffered from high blood pressure, heart disease, and other ailments. Sometimes when a slight illness appeared he would devoutly recite the holy name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and beseech the Bodhisattva in compassion to save him from suffering. Once in a dream he saw Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva treat him and sprinkle him with sweet dew, and his illness was cured at once. In recent years his body grew stronger by the day and his face glowed. He rarely needed injections or medicine — this is a fact. Ours is a Buddhist family; the whole household believes in the Buddha. My grandmother and maternal grandmother were devout believers in their lifetimes, and last August my mother received the lay Bodhisattva precepts at Banruo Temple in Changchun. My eldest sister and I

received and observed the Five Precepts, and though my second sister and my elder brother each have their own households, they took refuge in the Buddhist gate many years ago. Sometimes my mother would remind my father to attend to his Buddha-recitation, fearing that once well he would grow slack. My father would say: “I cannot let it slip — set your minds at ease. When I am not reciting aloud I am still reciting in my heart. When I go I will commit no offense; I will pass away easily and freely, free of the suffering of illness, and be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and my grade will not be low! There will be relics too — you will see. I have no concern for anyone in this family, because you understand the Dharma deeply and will handle everything well. In our family I will be the first to go; afterwards we shall all meet in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. You must recite the Buddha's name well — it brings great real benefit….” He said a great many things in joyful longing for rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (he often spoke this way).
This year, in the
eighth
month, on the
12th

(the fourteenth day of the seventh lunar month), at a quarter past midnight, (my father's) breathing became somewhat hurried. My elder brother was sleeping beside him; hearing the sound, he quickly turned on the light to look. Seeing the state he was in, he urgently called the family to rise and recite for him to assist. He himself recited silently along with everyone, and a few minutes later, amid the sound of the assembly reciting the Buddha's name, he passed away peacefully in the West. His face bore a smile, serene and at ease, his complexion ruddy; all who saw him praised it. Eight hours later, when the burial clothes were put on, his limbs were supple and his skin fair. The masters of Jile Temple and some of the lay Buddhists came to chant sutras (and more than a hundred relatives saw it as witness). The family did not wail or weep then; the coffin lay at home for three days with sutra chanting and Buddha-recitation day and night. On the evening of the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month, at Harbin Jile Temple, the precepts of the Bodhisattva for the dead were conferred on my father; on the sixteenth he was cremated bearing the precept body. A white heart-shaped śarīra was obtained, along with many śarīra flowers and many firm relics large and small. The bone powder showed seven colours — pink, green, yellow, grey, black, orange-red, and white, in the shape of coral — and all who saw it marvelled.
Gu Fengzhu, Administrative Section, Harbin Municipal Water Company,
