tenth
month, on the
11th
day

blocks.text: 1. Passing Away with a Smile While Reciting the Buddha's Name

inline.s: (Original title: Xu Guozhi's Mother Gives Everything She Has for Disaster Relief and Passes Away Smiling While Reciting the Buddha's Name)

All living beings possess the Buddha-nature. Therefore, whether they be gods, humans, asuras, ghosts, animals, or hell-beings — let alone distinctions of male and female, noble and base, wise and foolish, worthy and unworthy — their rising and sinking through the six paths, their ceaseless turning in birth and death, come about from the depth of their delusion and the good or evil of their karma acting as causes and conditions; yet their single thought of Buddha-nature is certainly never increased or diminished by this. Because they are deluded and do not know it, they not only fail to receive its benefit but on the contrary, relying on the power of this Buddha-nature's merit, give rise to delusion and create karma, and through karma bring on the root of suffering — is this not greatly to be pitied? The Tathāgata, in compassion, causes them to turn back from delusion to enlightenment, cut off delusion and realize the truth, until they personally realize the Buddha-nature inherently theirs. And because living beings lack the strength to cut off delusion — so that even with cultivation they cannot in this present life end birth and death, and having once more received a birth they are mostly lost, so that to the end of the future their liberation has no term — therefore, in great compassion, he specially opened the one Dharma gate of faith and vow, Buddha-recitation, and seeking birth in the West, so that all, whether ordinary or sage, may in this present life rely on the Buddha's compassionate power and escape birth and death. Compared with those who rely solely on their own power, the difficulty and ease, the slowness and speed, are as far apart as heaven and an abyss. Hence from ancient times to the present, of the four assemblies of monks and laity who cultivate this Dharma gate and are reborn in the West, there is no end to their number; even in recent times they are often seen.

The Lady Yang, mother of Xu, of Shitai County in Anhui, was the birth mother of Layman Xu Guozhi. In temperament she was filial, kind, gentle, and good, bright, keen, and decisive. In serving her parents, serving her parents-in-law, supporting her husband and teaching her children, managing the household and conducting affairs, in every respect she was a model for the inner chambers and a pattern for womankind; compared with the ancient biographies of virtuous women, of motherly exemplars, of the benevolent and wise, she is scarcely to be ashamed. She took up the Buddhist faith in childhood and became all the more firm in old age. She had three sons — Guohua, Guojun, and Guozhi — each holding office in government or business. Guozhi was in Tianjin and wished to serve at her side for long, so in

he brought her to Tianjin to care for her, whereupon she took up a lifelong vegetarian diet and received the upāsikā precepts. From then on she recited the Buddha's name with ever greater diligence and had many auspicious omens; but lest foolish people who do not seek single-mindedness and merely hanker after auspicious signs be harmed, these are not recorded. That autumn, Anhui suffered a rare calamity of flood and drought, and the provincial governor telegraphed for Guozhi to assist in directing relief work, because of the results he had achieved during eight years in the capital. Guozhi could not bear to go far from her, but the Lady, reproving him with the greater righteousness, urged him to go quickly and save the suffering people. While Guozhi was in Anhui for over a year, the Lady fell ill but would not allow any letter to mention it, fearing that he would come to attend her from afar and so delay the relief work. She also instructed Guohua and Guojun to solicit contributions, and gave her own private savings, emptying her purse to help; in recognition the President inscribed a plaque for her and bestowed the Compassionate Beneficence Badge. In the second year, when the relief work was done, the Anhui authorities still wanted Guozhi to stay, so he again brought her to Anhui to care for her. As she was already seventy-four and her vitality failing, some among the relatives urged her to give up the vegetarian diet. The Lady said: I would rather eat vegetarian food and die than eat meat and live. This spring her illness grew worse by the day, yet her mind was clear and she recited the Buddha's name without pause. She said to Guozhi: In worldly affairs I have tasted every hardship, and so I have no attachment; in my heart there is only the one matter of Buddha-recitation. She also said: Whenever fever comes the pain is extraordinary, but the moment I think of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss I feel cool and refreshed at once. On the twenty-first day of the second month she had monks invited to the house to recite the Buddha's name and assist her rebirth. She had all her own clothing and belongings sold and the proceeds offered to the Three Jewels. She asked Guozhi: Which day would be best to go? Guozhi answered that the day after tomorrow was a fast day and would be best. After some hours she said: I have already seen Shakyamuni Buddha and the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas enshrined in Tianjin — why is it that I do not see the Buddha who comes to welcome me? Guozhi said: When the time comes, you will see him. The next day she again recited the Buddha's name with the monks. At dawn on the twenty-third, the monk Fuhai, who was reciting for her, said: The Lady's mind and bearing are as usual; she cannot go within a day or two. By the hour of the snake, Guozhi invited a statue of the Welcoming Buddha to be placed before her bed and said, Amitabha Buddha has come. When the Lady heard this she was filled with great joy; she sat up and gazed at it, cried aloud several times, Namo Amitabha Buddha, then formed the mudrā and passed away with a smile.

Guozhi, with the masters and the family, went on reciting the Buddha's name aloud for three hours before they began to mourn, and then bathed and changed her. The fragrance was rich; a friend who came to offer condolences smelled it outside the door and exclaimed that it was rare. On the third day she was placed in the coffin, and her countenance was even more radiant than in life; the crown of her head was still slightly warm. Her four limbs were supple, and when a rosary was placed in her hand she still bent her fingers and held it. How admirable, how excellent! A woman such as the Lady may be called one whose roots from former lives were deep and whose present practice was pure, and who moreover had her son Guozhi to assist her in many ways, so that her pure karma ripened and she obtained the vow of swift rebirth. Of worldly people who do not recite the Buddha's name there is no need to speak; but even of those who recite with all their hearts, most of their children, at the point of death, wail, wash the body, change the clothes, and so on, causing the dying one both grief and anger, so that right mindfulness is lost and they must once more turn for endless kalpas through the three evil paths and the six realms with no way out. Yet such children still call themselves filial, not knowing that the offense of ruining a parent's rebirth is graver than killing them — and the whole world does not know it. Truly this is cause for sorrow. Guozhi's mother was kind and reverent and served the Buddha, and so she kept the fast and studied Buddhism all her life; and she repeatedly managed relief work, exhausting her heart and strength each time. This summer he came to the mountain and showed me an account of the Lady's life, asking me to write a record of it as a model for later generations of descendants. I declined on the grounds of my own dullness and pressing business, but he asked again by letter, and so I have set down her life in brief, and added somewhat more detail on the closing events, hoping that those who are mothers and those who are sons in the world may all take her as their pattern.
(Original title: Layman Jiang Qicheng Bows to the Buddha and Chants Sutras, and Passes Away Peacefully)

The Lady Jiang was a native of Xutong Village in the southern countryside of Dantu. Her family's ancestral home was in Donggou Village two li or so from my own, and she was born in the same year as I. While we were still in swaddling clothes our families arranged a betrothal, and we took refuge together, lodging at Rugao. When she was fourteen my late mother, the Lady Wei, passed away, and my two elder brothers died one after another; the household needing someone to manage it, the Lady was brought home. Three years later we were married, and I soon left with my books to study under a teacher, and thereafter made my living in all four directions. My late father, Lord Xuan, was growing old, and within the household, affairs great and small were all entrusted to the Lady. She drew water and ground grain with her own hands, economized on clothes and food, and managed the fields and houses inherited from our ancestors without the least disorder; her kin all called her worthy. In the autumn of the gengwu year she took refuge with Dharma Master Yinguang and was given the Dharma name Qicheng. From then on she bowed to the Buddha and chanted sutras morning and evening and kept a lifelong vegetarian diet. In the winter of the dingchou year she fled the turmoil and moved to Shuangdian Town. The following spring she moved again to Shiba Township south of the town, and there her heart and strength were utterly spent; her illness had its root from that time. Life grew harder by the day and her body weaker by the day. In the spring of the xinsi year she grew worse still, and lingered until the hour of the snake on the twenty-third day of the intercalary sixth month, when, amid the sound of the family reciting the Buddha's name in unison, she passed away peacefully. Her crown remained warm for several hours — sure proof of birth in the West. She lived sixty-two years.
Respectfully narrated by Shen Rujin and recorded by Shen Xiaoyuan, in mid-spring of the jiashen year
(Original title: Wu Huifang's Mother Foreknows the Time and Renders Up Her Retribution with Composure)

Wu Yuefang, a native of Nijiazhuang in Ren County, Hebei, is now the head of the Xingtai Pure Karma Buddha-Recitation Society. His entry into the Buddhist faith came about through joining the Tongshan Society, then passing step by step into the Buddhist gate; he took refuge with the Thirteenth Patriarch, the great master Yinguang of Lingyan, and was given the Dharma name Huifang. His mother, the Lady Hao, was advanced in years, and he explained the true Dharma to her and had her recite the Buddha's name constantly. In the autumn of the twenty-seventh year of the Republic his mother fell ill, and he knelt by her bed day and night, reciting for her the five Pure Land sutras, the Diamond Sutra, the Kṣitigarbha Sutra, the Great Compassion Mantra, and the Rebirth Mantra. Fearing that his mother's pure mindfulness might lapse and her rebirth be spoiled, he agreed with her beforehand that during the recitation, whenever the word “Buddha” occurred, he would strike the gong once and she would recite Amitabha once, so that she might keep to the agreement and not lose the great name. Her diarrhea lasted for days and she grew thin as firewood. Knowing she could not be cured, he took leave of his mother for Xingtai to buy grave clothes and coverlets. As he was leaving he instructed his elder brother and sister-in-law to recite the Buddha's name well for her and have their mother follow along, and told them that when her life ended they must not panic but must follow the Ferry-Boat at the Time of Death and carry it out with care.

When his mother's illness became critical she called her granddaughter to her and had her wash and wipe her whole body clean, saying, I shall die tomorrow. And indeed at the hour of the dog on the twelfth day of the ninth month she calmly rendered up her retribution. Huifang returned only on the thirteenth and did not see his mother; his grief tore him apart inside. But he heard that at the end she was composed, her body cold and her crown warm — surely born in the West. Huifang, with the family, again recited the Buddha's name and turned the merit over to his mother, hoping that her grade in the lotus might be raised. At night he dreamed of his mother, her countenance fresh and lovely, her smile beaming. Startled and overjoyed, Huifang asked her, Mother, do you come reciting the Buddha's name? His mother said, I recite the Buddha's name. Recite it for me. His mother at once recited after him, Namo Amitabha Buddha. Huifang was overjoyed, and suddenly woke to find it a dream; he knew that his mother was certainly born in the Western Pure Land. Mother Wu was compassionate and kind, loving all living beings without exception, and never in her life ate fish or shrimp (her village stands among the northern marshes, where fish and shrimp are plentiful, so abstaining was hard), and therefore she was free of illness all her life. At the end someone mistakenly offered her a meat bun, which she spat out the moment it touched her lips. It is clear that her virtue of precepts was long matured and unlike the common run. Old and young in the family all believe in the Buddha. Her father, Wu Tingjun, took refuge with the monk Xuyun, and the family was Buddhist throughout.
Recorded by Chang Huiyang

blocks.text: 4. Passing to the West in Peace

inline.s: (Original title: Zhang Zhirao's Mother Never Lets the Buddha's Name Leave Her Lips and Passes to the West in Peace)

Liankai and Layman Zhang Zhirao were flesh and blood in the Dharma gate. Zhirao was a native of Suzhou and did business in Bengbu, and when Liankai had occasion to go to Bengbu he always lodged at his house. He saw that within the family all was reverent, harmonious, and at peace, and that Zhirao's mother, the Lady Zhao, now well past eighty, held a string of beads in her hand and never let the Buddha's name leave her lips. In his heart he wondered and revered her. Zhirao had taken refuge with the aged Master Yin for many years; out of deep gratitude for his mother's kindness he made the pure karma the expression of his filial thought, and so moved the old lady to faith, and in the twenty-eighth year she too wrote asking to take refuge. The Lady was kind, gentle, sincere, and plain, and thus already close to the pure karma; having received and upheld the Pure Land Dharma gate, she believed deeply and vowed earnestly, her whole mind fixed on the West. And because the family was harmonious and grave, no miscellaneous affairs disturbed her mindfulness. Zhirao had lost his father early. The family was poor and he made his living by teaching. The Lady drew water and ground grain with her own hands; though the house was as bare as a hanging chime and even wild herbs ran short, she was cheerfully content, economized on clothes and food, and taught her sons by righteous principle. Zhirao and his four brothers all grew up under their mother's teaching and won reputations for worth. Zhirao, the youngest, was especially loved by the Lady.

This year the Lady turned eighty-one. On the thirteenth day of the eighth month she felt slightly unwell, and her children and grandchildren wanted to call a physician. But the Lady stopped them and only recited the Buddha's name without pause. Zhirao knew something was different and gathered people to assist the recitation. It was Zhirao's thought that, as the Master had taught, the method of assisting recitation means that when the retribution is exhausted one is reborn, and when it is not exhausted the illness may quickly be cured. His mother, though advanced in years, was only lightly ill; yielding to the old lady's wish and assisting the recitation, he might well hope that her span was not yet ended and that she would recover. Who could have known that the Lady's pure karma was ripe and her Sahā retribution exhausted, and that amid the sound of the assisted recitation she would pass peacefully to the West — at the hour of the pig on the thirteenth. From the showing of illness to the giving up of retribution was only half a day, with children and grandchildren filling the room before her and not the least attachment. Her utter freedom from entanglement is something even long cultivators may fail to match, and from this we may know the cultivation of former lives. And the way she conducted herself throughout life, everywhere a model for the inner chambers, truly had its source. Zhirao's filial thought is pure and deep; he restrained his grief and did everything according to the Master's Ferry-Boat at the Time of Death, in every respect according to the Dharma. In life he had done his utmost in caring for her bodily needs, and he was able to lead his mother to the world-transcending Dharma. In the rites at the end he did not take the coffin, grave clothes, and the display of funeral pomp as his utmost, but made it his aim that his mother be lodged in the lotus womb and dwell at ease in the treasure land. Alas, this is truly the great filial piety that transcends the world, a model for people everywhere. Moreover I would wish Zhirao to strive diligently in practice and make great vows, to spread the Dharma and benefit living beings, as the great filial piety that glorifies the world-transcending way. Then the Lady, in the seven-jewelled lotus pond, gazing far at her worthy son in the Sahā world, will smile with still greater joy.
Recorded by Liankai

blocks.text: 5. Welcomed by the Buddha with Fragrance Released

inline.s: (Original title: Ms. Yu Zhenghui Smiles and Joins Her Palms as the Buddha Welcomes Her and Fragrance Is Released)

At Gaoting Town on Daishan in Dinghai. Mrs. Yu, wife of Gu Huasun, was twenty-five. She had been ill for over a year, and medicine and treatment were of no avail. She was urged to recite the Buddha's name but did not believe, and her condition grew critical. Her husband Gu Huasun obtained Great Compassion water for her to drink and told her of the Bodhisattva's deeds in saving beings from suffering, and only then did she begin to recite the holy name of Avalokiteśvara. On the twenty-fourth day of the fifth month a seven-day Avalokiteśvara retreat was begun at the Lay Buddhists' Forest, with the great master Shanhui presiding, and since the lady had no strength to come to the Forest she recited the holy name silently from her sickbed, and a picture of Amitabha welcoming and guiding was hung in her room as well. Her husband also explained to her the splendours of the Western Land, the merits of Amitabha, the causes and conditions of rebirth, and the three essentials at the time of death spoken by Master Yin in the Ferry-Boat at the Time of Death, opening and guiding her again and again. At his words the lady had a great awakening. She said: “From now on I put down all conditions and single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name. Though Zongjian is only seven (meaning her son), he is clever and lively and has his father to rely on — what have I to worry about in dying?” From then on she never spoke of family matters, and whenever anyone came to see her she would earnestly beg them to recite the Buddha's name. She said: When I hear the Buddha's name my heart feels joy. When the seven-day period was completed she took refuge with Master Shanhui and was given the Dharma name Zhenghui.

On the eighth day of the sixth month she suddenly began reciting the Buddha's name aloud and clearly without pause for forty minutes together. On the morning of the tenth she said to her husband Gu: Last night the Buddha came. Gu told her that if she saw the Buddha again she should ask the time of her birth in the West and prepare for what was to come, and the lady agreed. Some two hours later she said with a smile: I have obtained the water of the eight merits; give it to me quickly to drink. Gu suspected delirium and gave her the Great Compassion water. The moment she swallowed it she said: That is not it. Glancing at the bedside she said, The cup of water is here, and drank it. Delighted, she said, How fragrant, fresh, and sweet this is! He asked when she had been to the West. She said, Just now I went to the West and saw the Buddha on a lotus flower in the jewelled pond; the water of the pond was clear and lovely, and surely it can cure my throat ailment. So I asked the Buddha for water, and the Buddha had someone ladle out half a cup and set it on the second step. I was afraid of spilling it if I drank there, so I carried it back, never expecting it to be so wonderful. She had also asked the Buddha when he would in compassion come to welcome her, and he indicated tonight; and so she asked her fellow practitioners to begin the assisted recitation. The lady suddenly smiled, joined her palms, and bowed, to everyone's astonishment (for her arms had long been useless from illness and had no strength to move). As the night deepened she said with another smile: The Buddha has come; I am going. At that moment a rare fragrance was suddenly smelled, far surpassing sandalwood or musk. Everyone stood in reverence, and the lady herself straightened her body and arranged her clothes and recited the Buddha's name along with them. When her breath was about to cease she suddenly turned onto her right side and passed away in the auspicious posture. The time was
, in the
sixth
month, on the
11th

day, at four in the morning. By nine o'clock her whole body was cold, but the crown of her head was still warm. There was a second death that day, and by custom the body was laid out. On the morning of the twelfth she was washed and changed; her body was supple, her lips red, her face as in life. Such auspicious signs are sure proof of birth in the West. I have therefore recorded them, to make manifest the Buddha's grace and strengthen pure faith.

Note: The lady's auspicious signs at death were manifest and were further confirmed by a reply from Dharma Master Yinguang; there is no doubt that she was born in the West. Yet though she was by nature obstinate, that too was the working of a firm and strong character; she was not to be compared with the wavering and the doubting. Her former disbelief in the Buddha Dharma came of not knowing Buddhist principle; hence once it was explained to her her faith and vow stood firm as none other's, and her courage and diligence were beyond the reach of others. Moreover Gu Huasun had long since taken refuge with Master Yinguang, was given the Dharma name Zongyuan, and kept a lifelong vegetarian diet and a fixed daily practice of Buddha-recitation. Influenced by him, the lady had in the spring of last year also made the vow to keep a vegetarian diet in gratitude to her mother. In the last few days before her death she took off the gold ring she wore of her own accord, saying, When I die I shall be born in the West; I have no need of this. She had already broken through greed and delusion and accomplished pure mindfulness. The sutras say that even the ten evil deeds and the five deadly sins may still attain rebirth carrying their karma — how much more so a lady of deep good roots and complete causes and conditions.
Recorded by Benru
(Original title: Wang Huizheng Puts Down All Conditions and Single-Mindedly Recites the Buddha's Name)
My late sister, the upāsikā Tang Wang Huizheng

She was the fourth daughter of my late father. In her young years she was bright and quick, uniquely gifted. While my late grandmother was still alive she served the Buddha with the utmost reverence, bowing and reciting morning and evening, and my sister, seeing and hearing it daily, was imbued from early on with faith. At twenty-two she married Mr. Tang Xianting of Yin County. The couple were harmonious and respected each other like guests; she served her mother-in-law with filial piety and treated those below her with kindness. Relatives near and far all called her worthy. Deeply planting the roots of virtue and long delighting in the joy of Chan, she came to realize the unreality of human life, its suffering, emptiness, and absence of self. At thirty-six she took up a lifelong vegetarian diet and served the Buddha, cherishing the aspiration to leave the dust, and devoutly cultivated the pure karma. She was sparing toward herself, looked on others as though they were wounded, gave with all her strength, and felt that the days were not long enough.

, during the August 13 Incident, when she returned from Linqing and saw refugees filling the roads, she took out the cloth she had brought and sewed garments by hand, giving them all away before she stopped. In winter she sorted out her cold-weather clothes, giving the good ones to others and keeping the worn ones for herself. When people asked why, she said: I grieve for those poor folk, anxious and unsettled — what time have they to sew?

she took refuge with the great master of the Pure Land school, Master Yin, who bestowed on her the name Huizheng, and at the same time she received the Five Precepts. From then on she was all the more courageous, the Buddha's name never leaving her lips. On the ten fast days she recited the Kṣitigarbha Sutra, and for ten years she never once broke off. But her constitution had always been weak and she had long suffered from asthma; add to this her toil in managing the household and her bitter, strenuous cultivation, and her health could not but suffer. In recent years the land was everywhere at war and devastation met the eye on every side; my late sister, whose heart was full of compassion, was deeply shaken, and her old illness returned, her face and eyes swelling. From the eighth day of the first month this year, after bowing and reciting, she lay exhausted in bed and could no longer bow and recite, only joining her palms in bed and holding the name. Shengzhao, out of deep affection between sisters, attended her sickbed for a long time. Grieving at her suffering, she prayed before the Buddha that if her allotted span were not yet exhausted the Buddha's grace might be added to her and she be spared medicine and recover early; and that if her span were exhausted, she might be received and guided to rebirth in the Land of Nurturing. My late sister knew she would not rise again; she put down all conditions and single-mindedly recited the Buddha's name, and for two months had asked nothing of worldly affairs. Hearing talk of idle matters around her, she would shake her head and say: Is it not better to recite the Buddha's name? Lying long, she developed bedsores, yet she always rose to urinate, and so kept herself clean. Before noon on the twentieth day of the third month, making the motion of striking the small gong and the wooden fish with her hand, she recited the Amitabha Sutra aloud to the end, then said she wished to recite the Great Repentance Text of the Eighty-Eight Buddhas, but stopped for lack of strength. At four in the afternoon her eldest sister Deyi and her sister's husband Layman Lin Di'an came together to visit her. Her eldest sister took up the book Ferry-Boat at the Time of Death and had her read it. Her sister said: Two months ago my eyes were so dim I could see nothing — how can I now? As the words ended she tried to rise, and as she rose her head drooped to her breast; in that single instant she had been received and guided by the Compassionate Honoured One. Fourteen hours after her death her body was soft as cotton and the crown of her head still warm. She was placed in a jar. On the twenty-sixth, the first seventh day, in accordance with the Buddha's rule, she was cremated, and the family all stood to the leeward. When the fire was lit the wind suddenly shifted, and the smoke was pure white as cotton, curling slowly upward. The attendant said: White smoke like this is not found once in a hundred. Afterwards the bones were gathered into the urn and dozens of firm relics were obtained, round and fine as pearls. Surely it was through many years of cultivation and diligent Buddha-recitation that she had so outstanding an auspicious sign and so great a harvest today. She lived fifty-nine years. Her husband came from Weihai and had been with her only twenty days; he recited the Buddha's name with her to assist her right mindfulness. Her son Changli, seeking his mother's recovery, copied out several scrolls of the Avataṃsaka Sutra. The whole family deeply believes in the Buddha Dharma.
Recorded by Fang Shengzhao
(Original title: Laywoman Fu Jingde's Buddha-Recitation Never Ceases and Celestial Music Comes to Welcome Her)

The chaste widow was a native of Hezhen in Huai'an, Jiangsu. She lost her husband early and followed her husband's aunt in cultivating the pure karma and reciting the Buddha's name. She took refuge with the monk Daoguo and was given the name Jingde. She lived long at the Baizi Hall under her teacher Huizhen. Keeping her chastity and cultivating purity, her fine conduct and pure discipline were known throughout her home district. In her practice, besides the fixed morning and evening Buddha-recitation, she also read the great vehicle sutras. She could recite from memory many of the poems, verses, and recorded sayings of ancient worthies such as Ouyi and Chewu. Her wisdom was lofty and her diligence surpassed others, and all revered her. Two years ago, hearing that the aged Master Yin had passed away to the West, she felt all the more stirred to effort, and grieved that her karmic conditions were poor and she had not been able to draw near to him. She deeply reflected that the three realms have no peace and the four elements are false; apart from Buddha-recitation and seeking the West, all conditions are like a dream. And so she fixed her mind solely on rebirth.

Her body was always frail and she was often ill; last winter she contracted typhoid and lingered without recovery. This spring the lotus friends of the region went to visit her and encouraged her, saying: The West truly exists, and this world is truly suffering; you should recite Amitabha and make your own provision; weary of dwelling in the turbid world, seek rebirth in the Pure Land. They also said they had heard that Layman Jiang had gone to Baohua to seek the precepts and they did not know when he would return (referring to Jingxin). She said she feared she would go around the Buddha's birthday in the fourth month, and asked them all to help her along when the time came; everyone answered that there was nothing to worry about, and the chaste widow gave a laugh. From then on she spoke less and recited the Buddha's name more. Jingxin arrived at Cha Town on the second day of the fourth month, and on the seventh Jingde sent someone to invite her, and Jingxin went at once. Reaching the Baizi Hall she saw that the illness was grave, and so gave her the instructions in Master Yin's own words. Jingde said she had dreamed of Patriarch Yin three times in the night and was ashamed that she had no strength to repay his grace, and asked Jingxin to show her the method. She then instructed her mother, the Lady Luo, to give Jingxin fifty yuan, saying: This is the money with which Jingde repays this one retribution. I beg you, Layman, to make merit for me in the Patriarch Yin society, so that I may go at once to the West and attend on him. She also said she wanted to return to her family home to die, to avoid obstructive conditions (for there were many outside-path followers around the Baizi Hall), and Jingxin agreed and returned to the Forest. On the twelfth the chaste widow was taken home by her family. On the evening of the sixteenth her husband's younger brother asked for her, and on the seventeenth Jingxin and the others hurried to assist the recitation. That evening the chaste widow urged the lotus friends and her mother to dress her. When she was dressed she gave instructions about the cremation, saying: Leave no trace, hold no other ceremonial Buddhist rites, only recite the Buddha's name. She earnestly exhorted her mother to truly believe in the Buddha and by no means to believe in the Dao, and said that following Layman Jiang and the others in practice was not wrong. That said, she recited the Buddha's name silently and lay quietly resting. Suddenly she said, There is a lovely music in my ears, and when everyone heard it they recited all the more earnestly. At this time, though the chaste widow's tongue was already stiff, she could still keep pure mindfulness unbroken, reciting the Buddha's name distinctly right up to the giving up of her retribution, never letting the Buddha's voice cease. The whole household was forbidden to weep; they assisted the recitation for six hours, then tested her warmth: the whole body was cold, but the crown of her head was still warm. This surely showed the auspicious sign of rebirth in the West. The time was
, in the
fourth
month, on the
18th

day, at the hour of the ox; she was thirty-four years old. After giving up her retribution she sat facing west for two days. Right up to the time she was placed in the jar her face was as in life, and all who saw or heard of it marvelled. But the local people clung to custom and would not follow the cremation. It was agreed in public meeting to await the autumn, set up a stele, and build a tomb, to preserve her chastity forever.
Recorded by Jiang Jingxin of the Rebirth-Assistance Society, Zhulin Buddha-Recitation Hall
(Original title: Li Songying's Mother Joins Her Palms, Recites the Buddha's Name, and Departs with a Smile)

My late mother, the Lady Dai, was the eldest daughter of my maternal grandfather. The family had a scholarly tradition, and she was well versed in letters. She helped my father manage the household and had a manly spirit. In dealing with people she was all harmony and gentleness, and never used harsh words. Among kin and clan there was no one who did not respect her. From girlhood she believed in the Buddha, constantly chanting the Avalokiteśvara Sutra and observing the Avalokiteśvara fast and the Cundi fast, never breaking off for decades. I remember that when we brothers were small we all fell gravely and dangerously ill with measles. My mother stayed with us day and night, anxiety written on her face, devoutly reciting the holy name of Avalokiteśvara and the White-Robed Mantra, and we recovered completely. My mother's constitution had always been strong. After fifty she suffered from dysentery and was several times in danger, but each time recovered. After the upheaval, alas, she lived three years in the countryside and suffered much alarm, while I, her unfilial son Song, attended her there. In the winter of the thirtieth year we brothers discussed it and had a boat brought to carry our parents back to the city (Rugao), hoping they might live in peace; my father did not return because of some matter. As the boat passed Shuangdian Town east of the county, fighting suddenly broke out in the night, and no one slept all night

On the twenty-third day of the tenth lunar month they reached home. Because my father was in the countryside, every time she thought of him she wept. Earlier, while in the countryside, my mother had already suffered from diarrhea for more than a month
and her spirit had greatly failed
Song urged her to take medicine and be treated
but my mother said sorrowfully: I do not wish to drink bitter water; I shall simply leave it to Heaven.

On the day of the winter solstice she still bowed to the Buddha and to the ancestors, her spirit as usual. Early on the seventh, she was suddenly greatly agitated by a family matter; that night high fever and chills came on violently and she vomited without cease, though the family did not yet know. Early on the eighth, when Song went to her room to inquire after her, he learned of it for the first time. Her mind was already unclear, and he at once had the family recite the Buddha's name in unison. That evening she suddenly became lucid and said, Last night my very bones were shaken apart, and asked for tea. When Song and the others heard their mother speak they were startled and glad
thinking there was hope of a turn for the better. On the ninth, tenth, and eleventh, for three days, there was no change. On the night of the eleventh
the situation changed greatly. After twelve o'clock

she had us unfilial ones come to her bedside and gave instructions one by one concerning family matters. She said to us: In life one must not be cunning and sly — “the more cunning and sly, the poorer one becomes.” If your destiny holds five pints, do not rise at the fifth watch; for if you rise at the fifth watch you will spill the five pints. All these were words urging goodness. She also bade us not to quarrel over the small things in the house, and to keep the family harmonious so that her heart might be at peace. Song and the others heard her with tears and agreed. At that time many laywomen from the Buddhist Lay Society came to see her off, reciting the Buddha's name aloud. The family recited along, and my mother joined her palms and recited with them. At midday on the twelfth she passed away with a smile, showing not the least sign of grief or suffering. The laywomen Zhao Defang and more than ten others all said that such an auspicious sign was exceedingly rare.
Respectfully recorded by her son Li Songying
(Original title: Laywoman Luo Jin Vows to Keep Chaste Widowhood, Maintains the Vegetarian Fast, and Recites the Buddha's Name)

The chaste widow Jin was a farmer's daughter from Tongli in Wujiang. She was widowed forty days after her marriage and vowed to keep her chastity. She supported herself by her own farming and for forty years never wavered. All her life she kept the vegetarian fast and recited the Buddha's name. She took refuge under the great master of Lingyan, Master Yin, and was given the Dharma name Jingde. In the gengchen year of the Republic (
) in winter
she died at the Zonghua Nunnery at Xiaoyan Ridge in Xukou

leaving instructions that her body be cremated. In the spring of the xinsi year she was cremated in the kiln at the Lingyan transformation site, and when the bones were gathered countless firm relics were found.
Recorded by Peng Wujin
(Original title: Laywoman Ma Juezhi Sits in Lotus Posture, Forms the Mudrā, Recites the Buddha's Name, and Passes Away Seated)

In Baoding, Hebei Province, the laywoman of the Ma family, née Yang, known by the Dharma name Juezhi, had ancestors from Shaoxing in Zhejiang who came to Baoding as secretaries to officials, and had been there for several generations. The family had declined, and she and her husband Ma Panqiu worked together in diligence and thrift and restored their former estate.

Panqiu died of illness, leaving two sons and two daughters, all still young; the funeral and everything else the laywoman bore alone. When Panqiu was gravely ill the laywoman had cut flesh from her thigh to mix with his medicine, yet the illness was never cured. After the burial she taught her sons and managed the household, all in good order. In her spare time she bowed to the Buddha and chanted sutras — this was how the laywoman began to study Buddhism. When her sons and daughters had married, the family gradually grew well off. The laywoman then devoted herself wholly to Buddha-recitation, morning and evening without a break.
It was not until

that the laywoman and her two sons together took refuge under Dharma Master Cizhou of Jinglian Temple in Beijing, and received the Five Precepts, being given the Dharma name Juezhi. From then on the whole family ate vegetarian and recited the Buddha's name, and became a Buddhist household. Apart from sleeping and eating, the laywoman sat cross-legged all day in bowing and recitation, and took no part in worldly affairs. In the spring of last year her second son Shixiong, through putting the official business in order and reciting with great ardour, fell ill from accumulated toil, yet still forced himself to attend to his duties. In the autumn he contracted diarrhea and could not rise; the signs at his death were excellent. But the family feared the laywoman would grieve at the news, and so kept it from her in silence. And her eldest daughter, married far away in Zhangyuan, had long not returned to visit. The laywoman had always cherished them dearly, yet of late she asked few questions about them, which shows that she had put everything down.

In this year, the renwu year, she was seventy-nine and her body gradually weakened. In the spring her skin began to peel, and by the first ten days of the sixth month it had peeled away entirely, revealing wholly new skin, fair and tender, not like an old woman's. In the middle ten days of the sixth month, after many days of diarrhea her vital energy was gravely damaged. The whole family recited the holy name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and she revived without harm. At about eleven in the morning on the third day of the seventh month, just as she was burning incense and bowing to the Buddha, she suddenly felt unwell, and the whole household again recited the holy name of Guanyin as a prayer. But the laywoman did not recite Guanyin; instead she herself cried aloud the name of Namo Amitabha Buddha — for she foreknew the time. After a while she rose of her own accord, sat cross-legged, and formed the Amitabha mudrā with her hands. She asked her family whether she was sitting well, and they all said she was sitting well. After that she did not move again

but went on reciting Amitabha Buddha as before, and the family all recited along. She asked not a single word about her children or household matters. Her manner was serene, and she showed not the least attachment. Presently she said suddenly, Light the lantern well and take it to the Buddha hall — the auspicious sign of death had already appeared. From then on her voice grew fainter, until at three in the afternoon, amid the sound of the assembly reciting the Buddha's name, she passed away seated upright. The fellow aspirants of the Buddha-recitation Hall, hearing the news, all hurried over and assisted the recitation in shifts. After several hours, warmth finally left her through the crown of her head

It was only around eleven that night that the body was laid down, changed, and placed in the coffin. Her four limbs were soft and clean, and there was no foul smell. From the ceasing of her breath to the placing in the coffin, eight hours passed, and she sat cross-legged as in life without the least change. There is no doubt that she was reborn in the Pure Land. The Buddha-recitation Hall was in the Red Guandi Temple inside Baoding city, a place where the faithful cultivated the pure karma together, and the laywoman was one of those believers. She was by nature sincere and warm, and in the home she could deepen the bonds of kinship and prosper the family business; in serving the Buddha she could strive with courage and diligence and transform the whole household; and at the end she removed every obstacle. Had she not been deep in bowing and recitation and great in the power of merit and virtue, how could she have come to this? Well did she deserve the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The ancient worthies said that with deep faith, earnest vows, and the holding of the name, rebirth is certain; the laywoman's case confirms it, and makes one believe it the more.
, summer — respectfully recorded by the colleagues of the Buddha-recitation Hall at the Red Guandi Temple in Baoding, Hebei.
(Original title: Laywoman Li Jingxiu Passes Away Peacefully Seated Amid the Sound of Buddha-Recitation)
The upāsikā Wang Li Jingxiu was a native of Licheng Town in Baoying, Jiangsu.
In the spring of 1937

she received the precepts at Mount Jiao. She had been introduced by letter by Jingxin to take refuge with the Thirteenth Patriarch of the Lotus School, the aged Dharma Master Yinguang, and was given the name Jingde. In her fifties, worn down by toil, she fell ill often. Hearing that the old man had passed to the West, her illness grew worse by the day. When she obtained the Record of Rebirth in the West, her illness improved somewhat. At the Zhulin memorial seven last year she vowed: If I can go within three years, I may call myself a disciple. Not long after, she hired a boat and came to Zhulin to have her long-life jar made (she had long since bought and kept one), and asked the boatmen to tell Jingxin to come out to Li. The four assemblies of the Forest all laughed and said: Laywoman Wang knows the date of her death; Jingxin agreed, saying, So she may.

On the thirteenth day of the first month this year Dai Jinglian, Fei Jingxing, and others came to Zhulin to join the society (the Perpetual Memorial Society) and also brought a letter from Jingxiu, urging Jingxin to come quickly to Li (at this time she was not yet ill). I asked the two of them whether she was ill, and they answered that she was fine, only that she wished me to come. On the fifteenth the Zhulin Ten Thousand Buddhas Good Karma Assembly concluded, and on the sixteenth I wrote a letter and gave it to the two of them to take. They reached Laywoman Wang's house only on the twenty-second. They read the letter aloud to her, and when they had finished she answered with the single phrase “Hard to meet without the condition,” and that was all. When the two took their leave she was still well. In the afternoon a slight illness appeared, and she said herself, Today I am not well. The family did not believe it, but by midnight she urged them to call the neighbours to assist the recitation. When the lotus friends nearby heard of it they all came eagerly. Jingxiu moved a wicker chair herself and sat upright facing west. She asked the lotus friends to assist her purely according to the method of assisted recitation in the Ferry-Boat at the Time of Death, and she herself recited along. Toward sunrise her filial son Jingji recited aloud at his mother's ear to assist. By then her breath was faint and only her lips moved. Then, amid the sound of the assembly reciting the Buddha's name, she passed peacefully to the West. It was

, at the hour of the dragon on the twenty-third day of the first lunar month. When she was examined, the whole body was cold and only the crown warm. In life she had been much ill, yet at death she was serene and gave no thought to worldly feelings. All these things prove that she foreknew the time, that her faculties were joyful, that her right mindfulness was clear, and that she gave up her retribution in peace as if entering Chan samādhi; there is no doubt that she was born in the West. From this, those near and far who saw and heard all gave rise to right faith. A woman such as this, who personally gained the real benefit of the Buddha Dharma, had a power to transform others not much less than that of the great masters. And her enjoyment after death far surpasses that of the great masters. I earnestly hope that those who do not yet believe in the Buddha Dharma will give rise to right faith, and that those who already believe will cultivate the Pure Land. For the Buddha Dharma is inconceivable, and Pure Land Buddha-recitation is especially inconceivable. The lady's case is clear proof of it.
Recorded by Jiang Jingxin
